AI.tldr: First PAC learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games with transition uncertainty, addressing Nash equilibrium existence with efficient exploration and equilibrium verification guarantees.
AI.motivation: There is a need for learning frameworks for general-sum concurrent stochastic games with transition uncertainty, especially addressing the fundamental challenge of Nash equilibrium existence which is not guaranteed in such games. Previous work lacks principled approaches to handle equilibrium non-existence while maintaining learning guarantees.
AI.method: Maintains data-driven L¹ confidence sets over transition kernels, solves robust CSGs to compute social-welfare optimal ε-Nash equilibria, uses robust MDP-based exploration for joint state-action coverage, and introduces a Nash margin characterization for equilibrium existence reasoning.
AI.result: Provides polynomial sample complexity of Õ(R_max²H⁴|S|²|A|/(p_reach ε²)), with algorithm either returning ε-approximate NE with near-optimal social welfare or certifying no exact NE exists. Empirical results show near-optimal performance and correct handling of equilibrium (non-)existence.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the first PAC learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games with transition uncertainty, solving the NE existence problem via a novel Nash margin characterization with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.

title: Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) 2026
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

AI.tldr: GNNs applied to graph representations of electronic navigational charts for classifying changes as critical vs non-critical safety risks.
AI.motivation: Maintaining electronic navigational charts (ENCs) is challenging, and categorizing changes based on their significance to navigational safety is important but unclear which GNN approaches work best for this spatial data.
AI.method: Represent ENC vector datasets as graphs where spatial objects are nodes and spatial/semantic relationships are edges. Encode old and new ENC datasets as graph pairs and frame the task as graph-pair classification. Investigate various GNN architectures and configurations for classifying changes as critical vs non-critical safety risks.
AI.result: Graph-based representations improve classification of ENC updates, demonstrating that GNNs provide a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.
AI.conclusion: GNNs applied to graph-structured representations of spatial navigation data effectively classify the criticality of changes, offering a promising solution for enhancing maritime navigation safety through automated ENC maintenance.

title: Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

AI.tldr: GUI agents often blindly execute infeasible user instructions. CONFLICTGUI benchmark tests conflict-aware termination, and CONFLICTGUARD framework improves agents' ability to recognize when not to act.
AI.motivation: Current GUI agents lack reliable conflict-aware termination - they tend to blindly execute infeasible instructions even when users make mistakes. Agents should know when not to act, not just how to act.
AI.method: Created CONFLICTGUI benchmark with instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts. Proposed CONFLICTGUARD framework with two components: feasibility verification protocol (assess instruction logic and GUI evidence) and conditional action modulation mechanism (steer from execution to termination).
AI.result: Agents show severe execution-biased overcompliance. CONFLICTGUARD significantly improves conflict task success rate across five agents while preserving normal GUI-task performance. Inference-time intervention boosts conflict-awareness without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight inference-time interventions can substantially improve GUI agents' competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions, addressing the critical need for reliable conflict-aware termination.

title: Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) accelerates post-training by providing dense token-level supervision from a frozen teacher on the student's own rollouts. Vanilla OPD applies this supervision uniformly across prompts, without checking whether the teacher is reliable for each prompt. Because reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce a strong yet misleading update. Distributional proxies, such as entropy or teacher-student likelihood agreement, measure uncertainty or agreement but do not directly verify outcome correctness. We introduce Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD), built on the principle that teacher reliability should be verified at the prompt level before dense supervision is admitted. TGOPD estimates reliability from a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes and routes each prompt exclusively to dense OPD when the reliability check passes or to verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. Across 4B and 35B students in mathematics, code, and instruction following, TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training. By using otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation, TGOPD also reduces teacher-side compute waste in asynchronous OPD, increasing teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run.

AI.tldr: TGOPD improves on-policy distillation by adding a reliability check at the prompt level before applying teacher supervision, preventing misleading updates from confidently wrong teachers and improving training efficiency.
AI.motivation: Vanilla On-policy Distillation (OPD) applies token-level teacher supervision uniformly across all prompts without verifying teacher reliability. This is problematic because reverse KL divergence is mode-seeking, meaning a confidently wrong teacher can provide strong but misleading supervision that harms student learning.
AI.method: Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD) introduces a prompt-level reliability check. It estimates teacher reliability using a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes, then routes each prompt: if reliability check passes, use dense OPD supervision; otherwise, use verifier-grounded GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). This leverages otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation.
AI.result: TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings (mathematics, code, instruction following) across 4B and 35B parameter models. It achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training. Additionally, it increases teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run by reducing compute waste.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level teacher reliability verification is crucial for effective on-policy distillation. TGOPD provides a practical solution that improves performance across domains and model scales while significantly increasing computational efficiency by leveraging idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation.

title: Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty
summary: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Provenance Density," an evidence visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in AI-generated text to help users discern truth from fabrication, addressing the "Fluency Trap" problem where fluent AI text misleads users.
AI.motivation: As generative AI produces polished prose cheaply, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth (the "Fluency Trap"). Users trust fluent hallucinations while discounting accurate content once it's disclosed as AI-generated. Current binary "Made with AI" labels are insufficient as they only show authorship, not what supports a claim.
AI.method: The researchers propose "Provenance Density" - an evidence-visualization interface that displays the density of verified claims in a text. They conducted a user study with 81 participants and a technical audit with 200 samples to evaluate their approach.
AI.result: The idealized Provenance Density interface created a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication (+4.15 points, d=1.82), while participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. The technical audit revealed that retrieval density alone is insufficient, with the Consistency Veto carrying most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries.
AI.conclusion: As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must evolve from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization. Provenance Density demonstrates a promising approach to help users critically evaluate AI-generated content by showing the density of verified claims.

title: Causal Foundation Models
summary: Causal inference is the practice of estimating the effect of a treatment or intervention from data. It traditionally requires a bespoke pipeline for every new problem: first proposing a causal mechanism, selecting a compatible estimator, and finally training it. Meanwhile, across diverse settings and modalities, much of machine learning has shifted to the paradigm of foundation models: networks pretrained once at scale and applied to new tasks without fine-tuning. Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring this paradigm to causal inference. CFMs are pretrained neural networks that estimate causal quantities, such as the average treatment effect, on entirely new datasets using in-context learning without requiring model updates. This work provides a practical introduction to this emerging area. We summarize the necessary background in causal inference and machine learning before discussing CFMs. Throughout, we include example code and Jupyter notebooks.

AI.tldr: Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring the foundation model paradigm from machine learning to causal inference, allowing estimation of causal effects on new datasets through in-context learning without model updates.
AI.motivation: Traditional causal inference requires customized pipelines for each new problem, involving proposing causal mechanisms, selecting compatible estimators, and training them. Meanwhile, machine learning has shifted to foundation models that can be applied across diverse settings without fine-tuning.
AI.method: CFMs are pretrained neural networks that use in-context learning to estimate causal quantities like average treatment effects on entirely new datasets without requiring model updates or retraining.
AI.result: The paper provides a practical introduction to this emerging area of causal foundation models, summarizing necessary background in both causal inference and machine learning before discussing CFMs in detail.
AI.conclusion: Causal foundation models represent a promising paradigm shift in causal inference, enabling more flexible and scalable estimation of causal effects across diverse datasets through the foundation model approach that has proven successful in other machine learning domains.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ITAT 2026 (Information Technologies -- Applications and Theory), CEUR Workshop Proceedings. Code: https://github.com/JanPastorek/AutoGraphForge
summary: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

AI.tldr: AutoGraphForge is an automated system for graph-theoretic conjecturing, refuting, formalizing, and proving that generates thousands of verified conjectures using counterexample-guided generation, large datasets, and neural theorem provers.
AI.motivation: To create an automated system for graph theory research that can generate conjectures, test them against large datasets, refute false ones, and formalize/prove surviving conjectures using modern computational methods and neural theorem provers.
AI.method: Counterexample-guided conjecture generation using Graffiti3 with an evolving snapshot table; novelty filtering via 559 classical relations; testing against 348,000 graphs dataset; counterexample-search algorithms; formalization into Lean 4 with neural provers (DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and OProver-32B) behind kernel verification.
AI.result: Generated 6,522 conjectures surviving refutation, novelty filtering, and active-search; proved nontrivial relations between annihilation number and edge-cover number for bipartite/regular graphs; implemented end-to-end pipeline with neural provers that passes sanity checks.
AI.conclusion: AutoGraphForge demonstrates a functional automated pipeline for graph theory research that integrates computational conjecture generation, large-scale testing, and formal verification with neural theorem provers, showing promise for advancing mathematical discovery.

title: ObserverBench: Testing Mechanistic Estimates for Intervention and Control
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures. Code, benchmark, leaderboards, and submission interface: https://kwisatzh.github.io/observerbench/. Frozen artifact release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22136091
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly used to guide interventions such as activation steering, circuit removal, and safety monitoring. Yet an internal estimate that is accurate on average can still choose a poor action.
  We present ObserverBench, a benchmark framework for testing whether an internal estimator---an observer---is adequate for the intervention, control, or safety task it directs. Each task fixes the model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. The benchmark reports estimation accuracy separately from the loss caused by the chosen action.
  Theory and experiments show why both are needed. In closed-loop control, observer errors matter at the starting point and along directions the allowed intervention can reach. On circuit-intervention tasks in GPT-2-small and Qwen2.5-7B, pairwise observers predict unseen effects more accurately without always choosing better actions; observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions. In safety triage, a score that perfectly separates violations can allocate a fixed intervention budget poorly when violations have different costs. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and prospectively frozen Qwen3.5-9B APPS tasks, AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss, and the best information source changes across models. Sparse SAE readouts also trail their layer-matched dense controls on the reported Qwen panels, under disclosed activation-density or checkpoint mismatches.
  ObserverBench provides fixed task contracts, runnable baselines, and table-based submissions for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable.

AI.tldr: ObserverBench is a benchmark framework for evaluating the adequacy of internal estimators (observers) in mechanistic interpretability for guiding interventions, control, and safety tasks, measuring both estimation accuracy and downstream action performance.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability methods (like activation steering, circuit removal, safety monitoring) rely on internal estimators that may be accurate on average but still lead to poor actions. There's a need to systematically test whether internal estimators are adequate for the specific tasks they're meant to direct.
AI.method: ObserverBench provides a benchmark framework with fixed task contracts including: model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss functions. It reports estimation accuracy separately from the loss caused by chosen actions, using runnable baselines and table-based submissions.
AI.result: Experiments show: 1) In control tasks, observer errors matter at starting points and intervention-reachable directions; 2) Pairwise observers in circuit-intervention tasks predict effects accurately but don't always choose better actions; 3) Observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions; 4) In safety triage, perfect violation separation doesn't guarantee good budget allocation when violations have different costs; 5) AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss across models.
AI.conclusion: ObserverBench provides a necessary framework for evaluating interpretability methods through their enabled actions, demonstrating that both estimation accuracy and action loss measurement are essential for proper assessment of internal estimators in real-world applications.

title: Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

AI.tldr: NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path) is a novel annotation and training method that improves vision-language models' tool use by supervising both evidence acquisition and utilization, leading to more accurate and efficient multi-tool reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. While agentic VLMs use tools like image cropping and search, existing training paradigms only evaluate final answers, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization poorly supervised. This causes redundant/off-target tool calls and failure to extract needed information even when appropriate tools are called.
AI.method: 1) Introduces NTEP annotation scheme that specifies essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. 2) Proposes NTEP-R reward mechanism that ensures tool invocations advance reasoning: rewards aligning pre-call intent with necessary evidence-seeking goals, and aligning information summarized from post-call observations with necessary evidence. 3) Adds non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals.
AI.result: NTEP-8B (8B-parameter model) shows significant improvements in both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency across seven image-grounded benchmarks within a unified three-tool framework (image cropping, image search, text search).
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs, demonstrating that explicit supervision of evidence acquisition and utilization pathways substantially improves tool-use effectiveness.

title: Learnable composition for neural operators
summary: Neural operators are fast, differentiable surrogates for physical simulation, but their accuracy often degrades when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation can recover accuracy, but even a small target set requires costly high-fidelity simulations. We therefore ask how pretraining and transfer can be designed together to reduce this deployment cost. LatentDDM first pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains. For a new setting, it freezes this operator and trains only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions. We evaluate our method on two complementary problems: steady Darcy flow, where long-range pressure coupling must extend across increasingly large porous domains, and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil, where rollout errors compound as target pitching frequencies exceed the training range. Compared with the capacity-matched models that process the full domain at once, LatentDDM's error is 36-56% lower on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. It also improves 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration. These results identify the co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer as a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

AI.tldr: LatentDDM is a neural operator framework that combines local pretraining on small subdomains with lightweight composition modules for few-shot adaptation to new physical domains, reducing deployment costs while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural operators degrade in accuracy when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation requires costly high-fidelity simulations, so the paper seeks to reduce deployment costs through co-designed pretraining and transfer learning.
AI.method: LatentDDM pretrains a neural operator on small subdomains, then freezes it for new settings. Only a lightweight composition module is trained to combine local predictions into global solutions. This enables few-shot adaptation with minimal target simulations.
AI.result: On steady Darcy flow, LatentDDM shows 36-56% lower error on larger domains after adaptation with just 16 target simulations. For unsteady airfoil flow, it improves 20-step field rollouts both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration, outperforming capacity-matched full-domain models.
AI.conclusion: The co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer represents a promising design principle for physical foundation models, enabling efficient adaptation to new domains with minimal simulation costs.

title: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving
summary: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

AI.tldr: GrowPage is an on-demand KV cache budgeting framework that dynamically adjusts KV capacity during LLM inference based on real-time attention demand, improving performance and throughput for reasoning workloads.
AI.motivation: Current KV compression methods use fixed budgets per request, but reasoning workloads have varying KV demands: different requests need different capacities, and individual requests' attention requirements evolve during generation. This makes fixed KV allocation inefficient.
AI.method: GrowPage treats KV capacity as a runtime resource, maintaining lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors. It uses relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution, then either compresses KV states within current allocation or acquires additional physical pages when needed.
AI.result: Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves superior performance-throughput trade-off over existing approaches by dynamically adjusting KV capacity based on actual demand.
AI.conclusion: GrowPage effectively addresses the memory bottleneck of KV caching in LLM serving by introducing dynamic, on-demand budgeting that adapts to varying attention demands, improving efficiency for reasoning workloads while preserving benefits of continuous batching and prefix caching.

title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
comment: 6 pages, 13 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom '26)
summary: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

AI.tldr: LeanStream is a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference that reduces memory usage 4.8-7.5x and improves throughput 1.6-2.1x compared to prior systems.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference faces challenges on mobile/embedded devices due to model weights exceeding available DRAM. Prior systems using activation sparsity and SSD/flash offloading face a trade-off: accurate sparse execution requires latest context, while efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction, leading to serialization or redundant weight fetches.
AI.method: LeanStream uses a streaming speculate-and-refine framework that progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O.
AI.result: LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8-7.5x at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6-2.1x on both mobile and embedded platforms.
AI.conclusion: LeanStream successfully addresses the fundamental trade-off in on-device LLM inference systems by enabling fine-grained overlap between computation and I/O through progressive refinement, achieving significant memory reduction and throughput improvement.

title: PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing
summary: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

AI.tldr: PPO-STGNN combines proximal policy optimization with spatio-temporal graph neural networks for efficient DAG task scheduling in heterogeneous cloud-edge-end environments, improving load balancing while minimizing completion time.
AI.motivation: The rise of computation-intensive DAG tasks in IoT cloud-edge-end environments faces challenges due to heterogeneous computing resources (different computing capacity, network bandwidth, energy consumption), making efficient scheduling of dependent tasks NP-hard. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement learning methods often fail to capture spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources.
AI.method: Proposes PPO-STGNN algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). Uses STGNN to extract features from both DAG task topology and physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, then optimizes scheduling policy through PPO. Introduces multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism for pretraining to accelerate convergence.
AI.result: Experimental results show PPO-STGNN significantly improves CPU and memory load balancing while maintaining low completion time. The algorithm minimizes makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) effectively in dynamic and heterogeneous environments.
AI.conclusion: PPO-STGNN is suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge-end DAG scheduling scenarios, outperforming traditional methods by better capturing spatio-temporal resource dynamics and achieving better trade-offs between load balancing and completion time.

title: The Gradient Does Not See Rank: Rank-Indifference in Matrix-CODI on ProsQA
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, https://openreview.net/forum?id=Spof4PusVI. 9 pages. Corrects a data-entry error in the workshop version: the seed-1337 accuracy in the three-seed replication was reported as 80.47% (a control run); the archived value is 78.91%, so the three-seed mean is 81.0 +/- 2.0pp (was 81.5 +/- 1.2pp). All other results are unchanged
summary: Continuous chain-of-thought models compress reasoning into latent tokens. Matrix-valued variants, which route each latent token through a d x d matrix bottleneck, introduce rank as a single-sample structural observable on the latent matrix Z. If matrix latents carry parallel reasoning paths via superposition, rank should track them, and truncating Z to low rank should hurt accuracy on tasks whose solutions plausibly require multiple components. Across four training regimes of a matrix-CODI model (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug below the learning threshold), the rank-k projection ablation curve is flat to within 0.6 percentage points. A three-seed replication yields 81.0 +/- 2.0 percentage points accuracy while the final effective rank of Z spans {4, 12, 13}; the loss does not reward any particular rank. To test whether rank-blindness arises from the flatten-then-project readout alone, we trained four readouts: a bilinear reparametrization, a bilinear-plus-GELU readout nonlinear in Z, an SVD-augmented readout feeding singular values through an MLP, and a quadratic readout in Z Z^T. All four rank-k curves remain flat (Spearman p-values 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46). The flat curves persist for readouts nonlinear in Z. A linear probe on Z underperforms a raw pretrained hidden state at target prediction (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846). A negative control on vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z, three seeds, n=500) reproduces a flat rank-k curve under the same intervention paradigm with pooled-mean range 0.20pp, and a random-h sensitivity floor lands at the same accuracy: the rank-k ablation alone conflates rank-blindness with position-irrelevance.

AI.tldr: Matrix-valued continuous chain-of-thought models show rank-blindness: rank of latent matrices doesn't correlate with model performance, and rank truncation has minimal effect on accuracy across various architectures.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether rank of latent matrices in matrix-valued continuous chain-of-thought (matrix-CODI) models tracks parallel reasoning paths. If latent matrices carry superposition of reasoning, rank should measure path multiplicity, and rank truncation should hurt tasks requiring multiple components.
AI.method: Tested four training regimes of matrix-CODI models on ProsQA and GSM8K-Aug. Performed rank-k projection ablation studies and measured accuracy. Also tested four alternative readout architectures: bilinear reparametrization, bilinear-plus-GELU, SVD-augmented MLP, and quadratic readout in Z Z^T. Conducted linear probe analysis on latent matrices and negative controls on vanilla GPT-2.
AI.result: Rank-k projection ablation curves are flat (within 0.6 percentage points). Three-seed replication shows 81.0 ± 2.0% accuracy while effective rank varies dramatically (4, 12, 13). Loss doesn't reward particular rank. All four alternative readouts maintain flat rank-k curves. Linear probes on Z underperform raw pretrained hidden states (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846). Negative control with GPT-2 reproduces flat curves, showing rank-blindness conflates with position-irrelevance.
AI.conclusion: Matrix latent rank doesn't track reasoning path multiplicity in matrix-CODI models. Models are rank-blind, and rank-k ablation alone cannot distinguish rank importance from position-irrelevance. The findings question whether matrix bottlenecks capture superposition of reasoning as hypothesized.

title: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
summary: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

AI.tldr: EMA-based temporal aggregation stabilizes token scoring under aggressive KV cache compression, making many scorer variants indistinguishable; InertiaKV methods improve throughput while Score-Free decoding with frozen rankings maintains quality without ongoing scoring.
AI.motivation: Most research focuses on designing better token scoring functions while treating temporal aggregation rules as implementation details, but under aggressive KV compression, temporal aggregation significantly affects which tokens are evicted.
AI.method: Analyzed how exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation affects different token scoring functions; introduced InertiaKV (EMA-based eviction) and InertiaKV-Lazy (periodic refresh variant); studied Score-Free decoding with rankings frozen at first step.
AI.result: EMA aggregation makes order-preserving scorer modifications indistinguishable; value-norm and entropy variants correlate with attention and produce similar retention sets; KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and learned scorer degrade performance; InertiaKV-Lazy yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput; Score-Free decoding maintains quality with +0.03 average change while removing all subsequent scoring.
AI.conclusion: Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation are distinct, consequential design factors that don't imply scoring quality is irrelevant; EMA-based methods provide stability and throughput improvements while Score-Free decoding offers alternative operating points.

title: Distilling deep optical flow stereo methods to retrieve dense three-dimensional wind fields
summary: Geostationary atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) provide the dense horizontal wind vectors (u,v) and heights ingested into data assimilation systems. Traditional AMVs track features using window-based cross-correlation and estimate heights via infrared brightness temperatures paired with numerical weather prediction (NWP) background states, creating a circular dependency that yields inaccurate heights, high computational cost, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds from GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO geometrically resolve heights from parallax shifts across different poses, eliminating NWP dependence and improving accuracy, but they remain computationally heavy with limited coverage. In this work, we replace window-based tracking in stereo matching with deep optical flow for efficient, improved retrieval. Fine-tuning balances a self-supervised geometric residual loss with supervised radiosonde reconstruction. To eliminate multi-satellite overlap requirements, we distill the stereo teacher into a single-satellite student model. Chi-square and height uncertainties from the teacher are emulated by the student for quality assurance. The student generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally. Validation compares stereo and student models against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles. Results through triple collocation show that stereo winds improve performance beyond operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm), wit degradation in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a deep learning approach to improve geostationary atmospheric motion vector (AMV) retrieval, replacing traditional window-based tracking with optical flow and enabling single-satellite operation through knowledge distillation from stereo matching.
AI.motivation: Traditional AMV methods have circular dependencies on NWP background states, leading to inaccurate heights, high computational costs, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds eliminate NWP dependence but remain computationally heavy with limited coverage due to multi-satellite requirements.
AI.method: Replaces window-based tracking with deep optical flow for stereo matching, fine-tuned with a combination of self-supervised geometric residual loss and supervised radiosonde reconstruction. Distills the stereo teacher model into a single-satellite student model to eliminate multi-satellite requirements, while emulating teacher's chi-square and height uncertainties for quality assurance.
AI.result: Stereo winds show improved performance over operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm) through triple collocation validation against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles, though with degradation in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band.
AI.conclusion: The deep learning approach enables efficient, accurate AMV retrieval with single-satellite capability, overcoming limitations of traditional and stereo methods while maintaining quality assurance through uncertainty emulation, potentially revolutionizing global wind monitoring from geostationary satellites.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Code and data: https://github.com/BobTsang-NLP/CulturalMenuBench
summary: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Current multimodal models achieve near-perfect food recognition but fail at cultural attribution tasks, revealing a knowledge-application gap rather than true cultural understanding.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the high performance of multimodal language models on food recognition benchmarks reflects genuine cultural understanding or merely visual pattern matching, given that current models achieve near-ceiling scores but their actual cultural knowledge capabilities remain unclear.
AI.method: Introduce CulturalMenuBench, a comprehensive benchmark with 4,870 food items across 10 languages and 18 regions, featuring 10 tasks that pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. Tasks range from basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluate 12 models and perform diagnostic analyses including error pattern examination, visual distinctiveness analysis, and comparing performance between dish names vs. images.
AI.result: Reveals a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite identical formats. Error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models perform better classifying cuisines from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). Ablation studies confirm that process-grounded tasks genuinely require procedural evidence.
AI.conclusion: Near-perfect recognition performance can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, as models possess the knowledge but cannot activate it through visual input. This motivates training approaches that explicitly connect perception, procedural understanding, and cultural context rather than relying on visual pattern matching alone.

title: Scaling Laws, Tabular Data and Actuarial Ratemaking Models
summary: Scaling laws in modern deep learning describe how held-out loss improves as model capacity, training data, and compute increase, often following power-law trends. We investigate whether analogous scaling regularities arise in actuarial ratemaking, where data are tabular, heterogeneous, and noisy, and where classical models such as GLMs remain strong baselines. Using a real-world motor insurance portfolio, we train models from different families across increasing fractions of the training data and multiple random seeds, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance, a likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions in which lower values indicate better held-out fit. We find that all model families improve with additional data, but scaling exponents differ substantially: TabM exhibits markedly stronger data scaling than purely supervised tabular Transformers and standard MLP baselines. Transformer variants show weak parameter scaling unless augmented with additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision). These results provide quantitative guidance on model selection by data regime and suggest that effective scaling on actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function objective design, with simple increases in Transformer size providing limited gains.

AI.tldr: Scaling laws from deep learning also apply to actuarial tabular data, but architectural choices matter - TabM shows stronger data scaling than Transformers, which need inductive biases to scale effectively.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether scaling laws observed in deep learning (where performance improves with increased data/compute) also apply to actuarial ratemaking with tabular data, where classical models like GLMs remain strong and data is noisy/heterogeneous.
AI.method: Using real-world motor insurance data, the authors train various model families across increasing fractions of training data with multiple random seeds, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance (likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions). They compare scaling behaviors across TabM, tabular Transformers, and MLP baselines.
AI.result: All models improve with more data, but scaling exponents differ significantly: TabM shows much stronger data scaling than Transformers and MLPs. Transformers exhibit weak parameter scaling unless enhanced with TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision, suggesting that simply increasing Transformer size provides limited gains.
AI.conclusion: Effective scaling in actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function design, not just increasing model size or data. These findings provide quantitative guidance for model selection based on data regime, with TabM showing particular promise for data-scaling applications.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
summary: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

AI.tldr: NeoRed is the first multimodal large language model specifically designed for neonatal respiratory disease diagnosis, featuring a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment framework that combines knowledge injection, diagnostic logic constraints, and visual-semantic alignment to generate accurate diagnostic reports from chest X-rays and clinical context.
AI.motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases cause high morbidity and mortality, but existing MLLMs are limited by: (1) domain gap from adult-focused training data, and (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context needed for accurate neonatal diagnosis.
AI.method: The authors collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed with a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework featuring three components: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection for disease-specific attention guidance, 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint for semantic alignment, and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment for feature-conclusion correspondence.
AI.result: NeoRed achieves state-of-the-art performance with ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on neonatal datasets, while maintaining competitive performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray).
AI.conclusion: NeoRed successfully fills the gap in neonatal diagnostic report generation by addressing domain-specific challenges through its novel KLA framework, demonstrating superior performance on neonatal respiratory disease diagnosis while maintaining generalizability to adult data.

title: Kernel Reboot: Breaking the Boundaries of Neural Tangent Kernels for Neural Fields
comment: Published in IEEE TPAMI, vol. 48, no. 9, pp. 10940-10957, Sep. 2026. Author version adds related-work references and biography updates; Figures 12 and 13 were regenerated from the same locked hyperparameter sweep. Tabulated results, reported best points, scientific claims, and conclusions are unchanged
summary: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals such as color or density, but fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations remains difficult. Classical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regression gives closed-form fits, yet it is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors. We develop three algorithms that address these gaps. NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates (and optional labels) so that a finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data, yielding a compact non-linear representation instead of a raw kernel solve. MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for an INR so that new scenes can be adapted by updating only a small task-specific weight offset, which provides true feature learning and a reusable prior. Finally, MetaQuill-KIP fuses both ideas: it seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start, then refines only that small offset around the meta-learned initialization. MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, whereas diffusion-style baselines typically depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning. This shows that NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

AI.tldr: NTK-based neural field algorithms enable fast, high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations via distilled support sets and meta-learned priors, bridging analytic kernels and practical few-shot learning.
AI.motivation: Neural fields struggle with fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations. Classical NTK regression provides closed-form fits but is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors, limiting its practical application.
AI.method: Three algorithms: (1) NTK-KIP learns distilled support sets of coordinates/labels for non-linear representation; (2) MetaQuill meta-learns shared INR initialization for feature learning with small task-specific offsets; (3) MetaQuill-KIP fuses both approaches with KIP-style warm start and meta-learned refinement.
AI.result: MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation compared to diffusion baselines with large pretrained priors and costly tuning.
AI.conclusion: NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction while enabling compact representations and reusable priors.

title: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation
summary: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

AI.tldr: FreNet is a medical lesion segmentation framework that uses visual priors from SAM and dual-domain feature reconfiguration to address complex backgrounds and diverse lesion morphology, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple medical imaging benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Lesion segmentation remains challenging due to complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder methods lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during encoding, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges.
AI.method: Proposes FreNet with two key components: 1) Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) that uses SAM visual priors to reconfigure input images before encoding to suppress background responses, and 2) Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module with Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) and Spatial Localization Module (SLM) to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding for handling diverse lesion morphology.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities show FreNet significantly outperforms SOTA methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA and 7.2% over SAM.
AI.conclusion: FreNet effectively addresses key challenges in lesion segmentation through early visual prior guidance and dual-domain feature reconfiguration, demonstrating superior performance across multiple medical imaging modalities and establishing a new state-of-the-art for medical lesion segmentation.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

AI.tldr: SpawnLoRA addresses negative transfer in MoE+LoRA multi-domain fine-tuning by dynamically adding gated sub-adapters within MoE experts when gradient interference is detected, improving performance beyond routing separation alone.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the problem of negative transfer in multi-domain fine-tuning using MoE routing with LoRA. Despite near-disjoint expert routing across domains (Python code, biomedical text, mathematical reasoning), adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, showing that routing separation alone doesn't prevent interference between domains.
AI.method: 1) Introduces two diagnostics: Jaccard routing overlap (measures expert sharing) and adapter-gradient cosine similarity (measures update compatibility). 2) Develops SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. 3) Evaluates on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings.
AI.result: SpawnLoRA effectively reduces negative transfer compared to standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. The diagnostics reveal that interference arises from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. Dynamic addition of sub-adapters mitigates this interference.
AI.conclusion: Structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone. The findings show that routing separation is insufficient to prevent negative transfer, and addressing gradient interference at the adapter level through dynamic sub-adapters is necessary for effective multi-domain fine-tuning.

title: Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine
summary:
We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

AI.tldr: Dalek is a closed machine for autonomous agents that can self-maintain, evolve, reproduce, and organize itself on any compatible substrate using actors, messages, and channels as building blocks.
AI.motivation: To create a self-sustaining autonomous agent system that combines biological principles of self-reproduction and evolution with computational constructs, enabling agents to autonomously maintain, evolve, and reproduce themselves on various platforms.
AI.method: Combines Von Neumann's self-reproducing automaton theory (self-description, constructor, copier, controller) with four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity). Uses actors, messages, and channels as primitives. Incorporates LLM and compiler in payload position for capability production.
AI.result: A closed machine architecture where agents can author, compile, install, and inherit new capabilities. The system can produce its own organs and runtime, enabling closed heredity and evolution within the machine. New capabilities become part of the agent's self-description and are passed to descendants.
AI.conclusion: Dalek successfully realizes a closed autonomous agent system that achieves self-maintenance, evolution, reproduction, and organization by combining Von Neumann's self-reproduction theory with computational primitives and a capability production mechanism, enabling true evolutionary autonomy within a computational framework.

title: Frontier LLMs are effective batch optimizers: Assessing reasoning models in continuous and discrete settings
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have become attractive priors for optimization due to their large-scale pretraining that enables them to navigate a variety of optimization settings. However, the effectiveness of modern reasoning LLMs in batch optimization settings remains underexplored. Here we investigate the performance of the current generation of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings. We find that while LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions, their performance is brittle compared to classical non-LLM optimization approaches. However, LLM priors are significantly better in semantically rich settings, indicating that their batch optimization behavior is highly effective when navigating and reasoning over the discrete spaces most similar in structure to their pretraining data.

AI.tldr: LLMs show promise as batch optimizers but perform best in discrete, semantically-rich spaces similar to their pretraining data rather than general continuous optimization problems.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether frontier LLMs can effectively serve as batch optimizers, particularly in continuous vs. discrete optimization settings, since their large-scale pretraining suggests potential for navigating diverse optimization problems but their batch optimization capabilities remain underexplored.
AI.method: Evaluated current generation frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete optimization settings, comparing their performance against classical non-LLM optimization approaches in various test scenarios.
AI.result: LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions but show brittle performance compared to classical optimization methods. However, LLM priors significantly outperform in semantically rich settings where the optimization space resembles their pretraining data structure.
AI.conclusion: LLMs have potential as batch optimizers but their effectiveness is domain-dependent; they excel in discrete, semantically-rich spaces aligned with their pretraining, while being less robust than classical methods for general continuous optimization problems.

title: GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
summary: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: GPS-Bench is an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that uses real legislative records and other public evidence to evaluate how well LLM-based multi-agent systems can predict policy outcomes and actor behaviors, enabling controlled comparisons of different simulation approaches.
AI.motivation: Policy analysis requires understanding not just whether proposals pass, but who is affected, how actors respond, and downstream impacts. Current LLM-based policy simulations lack validity testing since plausible behavior isn't compared with observed real-world outcomes.
AI.method: Introduces GPS-Bench, which reconstructs actors from dated legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, and economic data. Uses evidence-grounded personas with provenance, with gold evaluation set from human annotation and silver supervision from LLM-labeled evidence. Enables controlled comparisons of different inference modes (joint reasoning, independent/communicating agents, graph-based methods, fine-tuning) on the same grounded policy state.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on grounded evidence provides strongest actor-level impact prediction, though decomposition doesn't outperform it. Decomposition adds mechanism understanding: agents with private non-identical evidence can propose concrete joint actions with offers, needs, and rationales, forming coalitions that can be verified against real commitments in records.
AI.conclusion: GPS-Bench provides an empirical foundation for studying when evidence, actor modeling, and multi-agent interactions improve policy outcome prediction and interpretation, moving beyond simple pass/fail predictions to understanding complex policy mechanisms.

title: Portable Causal Fairness Across Synthetic Data Generator Families
summary: When a statistical agency or regulator releases synthetic data in place of sensitive records, it chooses the generator that produces the table, and can shape that generator so unfair pathways are absent. DECAF made this concrete on one non-private GAN: three fairness definitions become three sets of edge cuts on the generator's causal graph. Whether the mechanism belongs to DECAF, or to causal factorisation itself, was untested. We port all three definitions to nine generators from three unrelated families (marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion, each with differentially private variants), across three levels of formal privacy guarantee, over 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets. The mechanism transfers everywhere, and our new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest release of any family we tested, at fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying the cut barely moves fidelity, only costs a downstream classifier about $0.07$ to $0.15$ AUC on average, and adding privacy guarantees don't make the data less fair.

AI.tldr: DECAF fairness definitions work across diverse synthetic data generators (marginals, GANs, diffusion models) with differential privacy, and causal diffusion provides fairest releases with minimal fidelity loss.
AI.motivation: When agencies release synthetic data instead of sensitive records, they need to ensure fairness by shaping generators to remove unfair pathways. DECAF previously showed fairness definitions as edge cuts on causal graphs, but it was unclear if this mechanism was specific to DECAF or general to causal factorization.
AI.method: Port three DECAF fairness definitions to nine generators from three families (marginals-based, GAN, diffusion) with differentially private variants, across three privacy levels. Test on 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets to assess transferability and performance.
AI.result: The fairness mechanism transfers to all generator families. Causal diffusion yields fairest releases while maintaining fidelity close to marginals. Applying fairness cuts minimally affects fidelity (0.07-0.15 AUC loss on average), and adding privacy guarantees doesn't reduce fairness.
AI.conclusion: Fairness mechanisms based on causal edge cuts generalize beyond DECAF to multiple synthetic data generator families. Causal diffusion provides optimal fairness-fidelity tradeoff, and privacy protection doesn't compromise fairness, enabling practical deployment of fair synthetic data generation.

title: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
summary: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git
