Moreover, a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while leaving hard ones with too little computation. We introduce RecurTrace, which addresses both limitations using the loop's own trajectory. Specifically, Loop Memory Attention lets each looped layer attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, so the model can revisit earlier computations instead of relying on the latest state alone. A halting head then reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss. In a controlled MathQA comparison on the same looped backbone, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops. Finally, RecurTrace improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with the gain growing with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points.

AI.tldr: RecurTrace improves reasoning in language models by introducing loop memory attention to access earlier computations and adaptive halting to allocate depth based on input difficulty, outperforming fixed-loop and other adaptive methods.
AI.motivation: Existing latent recurrence methods have two key limitations: 1) each iteration can only see the previous output, losing access to earlier computations, and 2) fixed loop counts waste depth on easy inputs while providing insufficient computation for hard ones, limiting reasoning gains.
AI.method: RecurTrace introduces two main innovations: 1) Loop Memory Attention that allows each looped layer to attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, enabling revisiting earlier computations, and 2) a halting head that predicts whether to continue looping, supervised by an oracle identifying when additional depth reduces loss.
AI.result: On MathQA, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with average 2.0 loops, beating best fixed-loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. Outperforms ACT, PonderNet, CALM, LoopUS-Conf, and TaH-Mismatch baselines. Gains scale with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points improvement over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B models.
AI.conclusion: RecurTrace effectively addresses the limitations of latent recurrence by enabling access to earlier computations via loop memory attention and adaptive depth allocation via learned halting, resulting in improved reasoning performance that scales with model size while maintaining compute efficiency.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception
summary: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

AI.tldr: CauseCollab is a causal unified and modality-agnostic network for collaborative perception that addresses semantic inconsistency in heterogeneous multi-agent systems by disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific confounders through causal metric learning.
AI.motivation: Existing protocol-based two-stage methods for collaborative perception suffer from semantic inconsistency and error accumulation due to independently trained modality-specific converters generating modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, especially problematic in scenarios with large modality discrepancies.
AI.method: Proposes CauseCollab with two key components: 1) formulates representation learning in protocol space from causal perspective to explicitly disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning, and 2) adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. New modalities can be integrated by training minimal-parameter adapters.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.
AI.conclusion: CauseCollab effectively addresses semantic inconsistency in heterogeneous collaborative perception by providing a unified modality-agnostic framework that ensures semantic consistency across different sensor modalities and architectures through causal disentanglement.

title: TIGPO: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Graph-based policy optimization improves credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents by organizing rollout trajectories into state-transition graphs. However, existing methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. We propose \emph{Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization} (TIGPO), which extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates. TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task, allowing valid transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. To actively reconnect current exploration with historical experience, TIGPO allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots for ordinary task sampling and Revisit slots for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks. For each revisit, TIGPO pairs the current rollout group with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. The enlarged reference is designed to stabilize relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups, while comparison on the same task directly captures policy improvement across training stages. Historical transitions and scores serve only as structural and detached statistical references and are never replayed in the policy loss. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

AI.tldr: TIGPO extends graph-based policy optimization by maintaining persistent transition graphs across policy updates, using historical experience to improve credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based policy optimization methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions from earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small batch-local groups.
AI.method: TIGPO maintains persistent transition graphs for each task, uses a rollout budget split between Exploration and Revisit slots, creates cross-temporal references by pairing current rollouts with earlier Exploration groups, and uses historical transitions as structural references without replaying them in policy loss.
AI.result: TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Persistent temporal graphs that leverage historical experience across policy updates can significantly improve credit assignment and policy optimization for long-horizon LLM agents.

title: Semantic Bayesian World Models
summary: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs) - a probabilistic framework that transforms traditional knowledge graphs into belief networks, enabling unified reasoning with language models through Bayesian inference and semantic constraints.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental mismatch between knowledge graphs (which describe reality in crisp, deterministic assertions) and modern AI systems like foundation models and autonomous agents (which reason natively in probabilities). This mismatch prevents true integration, keeping knowledge graphs as mere data sources rather than enabling unified probabilistic reasoning architectures.
AI.method: The authors propose transforming the Web from a database of facts into a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs. Key methodological components include: ontological axioms constraining priors, observations updating beliefs through Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervening upon the world model. The approach involves belief annotation over RDF, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols for calibrated belief exchange between agents.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates potential benefits through conceptual examples: home-security agents probabilistically classifying gate figures (courier vs burglar), actuarial estimates aggregated by entailment rather than string frequency, planning tasks that language models typically fail, and estimation of quantities never explicitly stated in documents. The approach enables agents to reason about uncertain knowledge and coordinate beliefs.
AI.conclusion: Semantic Bayesian World Models represent a necessary evolution for knowledge representation, bridging the gap between deterministic knowledge graphs and probabilistic AI systems. This requires building new infrastructure including belief annotation standards, probabilistic reasoning frameworks, calibration mechanisms, and protocols for belief exchange to create a unified probabilistic-semantic Web for autonomous agents.

title: Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations
summary: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

AI.tldr: A graph-constrained agentic framework for adapting heterogeneous retail supply chain decision pipelines using LLMs, improving correctness and end-to-end success rates over direct LLM reformulation.
AI.motivation: Retail supply chains have coupled decision modules that need to adapt to evolving requirements. While LLMs offer natural-language interfaces for adaptation, existing methods focus only on individual optimization models and struggle with heterogeneous decision pipelines where requirements can have multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects.
AI.method: Formulate requirement-driven adaptation as joint selection of intervention routes and admissible module-level changes. Propose a graph-constrained agentic framework where domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces, and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100 warehouse requirements from practitioner interviews using GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek LLMs. Framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models compared to direct LLM reformulation, raising end-to-end success from 72-76% to 79-83%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed graph-constrained agentic framework effectively addresses the challenge of adapting heterogeneous decision pipelines in retail supply chains, outperforming direct LLM reformulation by systematically exploring intervention paths and leveraging domain-specific reformulation interfaces.

title: TraveL: Transformer-based Multi-view Path Distributional Representation Learning
summary: Path representation learning (PRL) for road networks has received increasing research attention, due to various path-related applications. Existing works on PRL typically exploit the co-occurrence relationship among road segments and paths to learn a vector as the path representation, without exploring the varied traveler behaviors and the regional correlation on the path. In this work, we propose to learn distributional representations, which provide valuable information for use in path-related applications, by capturing the varied traveler behaviors as well as the various dependencies within regions of road segments. We propose a novel Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning (TraveL) framework to encode a path along with a travel starting time to a distributional representation, which can be used to decode possible samples of on-path traveler behavior. Moreover, by analyzing the regional correlation which reveals various road segment relationships, we propose a regional attention to encode these correlations in a path. Also, we explore the idea of Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare the sampled traveler behavior against the collected ground truth to facilitate training. Experimental results show that the proposed TraveL model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, by 14.7% in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% in MAE for destination prediction.

AI.tldr: TraveL: A Transformer-based framework that learns distributional representations of paths by capturing varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations, outperforming existing methods on travel time distribution, path similarity, and destination prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing path representation learning methods only use co-occurrence relationships of road segments and paths, ignoring varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations within paths. This limits their effectiveness for path-related applications that require understanding traveler behavior patterns and spatial dependencies.
AI.method: Proposes TraveL framework with: 1) Transformer-based multi-view distributional representation learning to encode paths with travel starting times into distributional representations, 2) Regional attention mechanism to capture various road segment relationships within regions, 3) Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare sampled traveler behavior against ground truth during training.
AI.result: TraveL outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins: 14.7% improvement in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% improvement in MAE for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% improvement in MAE for destination prediction on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Learning distributional representations that capture varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations significantly improves path representation learning for road networks, enabling better performance on downstream path-related applications compared to existing vector-based approaches.

title: It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Also available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22261107. Code and pre-registered protocols: https://github.com/bulutyigit/problem-not-path
summary: Reasoning traces of large language models are widely read as containing "breakthrough" moments and early-legible fates. Both readings rest on measurements missing a counterfactual control at the level of the claim; we supply both controls. First, a restart-controlled truncation probe separates when a solution fits the continuation budget from when a prefix carries value that fresh computation cannot buy, comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched total generated-token budget. Applied to 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems x two small open models, an outcome-blind but difficulty-targeted cohort), exactly 1 of 178 cells survives as prefix-limited; restart dose-response separates a compute-starved model from a capability-limited one; and wherever the matched budget lies inside the restart grid, continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting (9 of 9) -- predominantly compute compression rather than expanded reachability. Second, a pre-registered, difficulty-controlled test finds no detectable outcome information in early-window internal signals beyond a problem-difficulty baseline, and two generation-free analyses of public corpora show why this control is needed: a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations -- inside the published probe range -- and a closely matched reconstruction of the closest published early-window positive recovers a comparable pooled result (0.849) while within problem it is statistically indistinguishable from chance at all ten anchors (0.496 at t=4); a post-hoc within-targeted probe finds only a small average residual, concentrated in three low-failure problems. High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is required.

AI.tldr: Two controlled analyses show that LLM reasoning traces: 1) contain little "prefix value" beyond compute compression, not expanded capability, and 2) lack early-window outcome information beyond difficulty baselines.
AI.motivation: To test two common readings of LLM reasoning traces: that they contain "breakthrough" moments showing early-legible fates, and that internal signals contain early outcome information. Both readings lack proper counterfactual controls.
AI.method: Two controlled methods: 1) Restart-controlled truncation probe comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restarts at matched token budgets, tested on 178 problem-model cells. 2) Pre-registered difficulty-controlled test plus generation-free analyses of public corpora including trace-blind difficulty proxy and within-problem evaluation.
AI.result: 1) Only 1 of 178 cells showed prefix-limited value; restart dose-response separates compute-starved vs capability-limited models; continuations beat restarts at matched budgets (9/9 cases). 2) No detectable outcome information beyond difficulty baseline; trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873, matching published probe results; within-problem analysis shows results indistinguishable from chance (0.496 at t=4).
AI.conclusion: LLM reasoning traces primarily reflect compute compression rather than expanded capability or early outcome information. High pooled probe AUROCs don't establish within-attempt information; proper controls (question-only baselines or within-problem evaluation) are essential for valid interpretation.

title: STAIR (STructure Aware Information Retriever): A novel dataset and LLM based retriever for document structure augmentation
summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a key component for generating accurate and hallucination free answers using Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs are improving at handling long context, but still suffer from "lost in the middle" problem. Thus, precise and accurate retrieval is important. Current retrievers chunk long context into length-based manageable chunks - in the process throwing away rich and informative semantic global structure in the corpus. We introduce a novel retrieval system STAIR that empowers an LLM to exploit global structure in a corpus such as a Table of Contents (ToC) to efficiently store and retrieve information from its model parameters. Our thorough and careful ablation studies with a finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system show that ToC helps build a low hallucination (less than 0.05%) generative Information Retrieval (IR) system and can generalize to examples where very few training samples are available. To further research in this novel direction of ToC based retrieval we release SearchTome - a diverse benchmark created from 18 books across 6 diverse domains to further research in this novel direction. STAIR achieves a high Recall@1 score of 82.6% on SearchTome as compared to DSI (76.9%), where the difference is found to be statistically significant. STAIR easily beats other strong baselines such as BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%) and out-of-the-box Mistral (13.8%).

AI.tldr: STAIR is a novel retrieval system that uses Table of Contents to leverage global semantic structure for more accurate RAG, significantly outperforming existing methods while reducing hallucination.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems chunk documents without preserving global semantic structure (like Table of Contents), losing valuable information and suffering from "lost in the middle" problems despite LLM improvements in handling long contexts.
AI.method: STAIR empowers LLMs to exploit global structure in corpora through a Table of Contents (ToC) approach using a finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system, enabling efficient storage and retrieval of information from model parameters.
AI.result: STAIR achieves 82.6% Recall@1 on SearchTome benchmark, significantly beating DSI (76.9%), BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%), and Mistral (13.8%). It reduces hallucination to less than 0.05% and generalizes well with few training samples.
AI.conclusion: ToC-based retrieval systems like STAIR offer a promising direction for improving RAG by preserving global semantic structure, enabling more accurate retrieval with minimal hallucination, and the SearchTome benchmark will facilitate further research in this area.

title: Guide, Not Bind: Why Defeasible Priors Fail in Augmented Lagrangian Causal Discovery
summary: Differentiable causal discovery methods increasingly encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints enforced by an Augmented Lagrangian (ALM) penalty, on the assumption that a data-adaptive relaxation mechanism will discount and eventually override a rule the data consistently contradicts. We show this design, which we call \emph{guide, not bind}, fails for two independent, precisely characterized reasons, and that directly repairing both restores it only partially. First, sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses a wrongly-forbidden true edge before any counterfactual check can detect it: we give three necessary conditions any adaptive relaxation must satisfy to avoid this (Proposition~\ref{prop:conditions}), prove that DADU---the natural relaxation rule this paper introduces as the object of study---violates all three (Corollary~\ref{cor:dadu_failure}), and confirm the failure across 3{,}072 training runs spanning graphs from 4 to 32 nodes, where a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge in 87--97\% of trials under DADU. Second, and independent of any fix to the mechanism, we prove in closed form that the standard correlation-matching objective ties a true edge and its reverse to an identical cost of exactly $2r^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tie}), not because the underlying equal-variance model is unidentifiable, but because normalizing to correlation discards exactly the variance information that would make it identifiable; covariance matching instead separates the two directions by a provable margin of at least $w_0^4$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:separation}).

AI.tldr: Differentiable causal discovery methods fail to properly handle forbidden-edge constraints using Augmented Lagrangian penalty because adaptive relaxation mechanisms suppress wrongly-forbidden edges too early, and correlation-matching objectives cause identifiability issues due to loss of variance information.
AI.motivation: Current differentiable causal discovery methods use expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints enforced by Augmented Lagrangian penalty, assuming data-adaptive relaxation will override incorrect constraints. However, this "guide, not bind" approach doesn't work as intended.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the failure through two approaches: 1) Examining sequential penalty-ramping ALM that suppresses wrongly-forbidden edges before counterfactual detection, identifying three necessary conditions for effective adaptive relaxation, 2) Analyzing correlation-matching objectives that create identifiability issues, and proposing covariance matching as an alternative.
AI.result: Two independent failures are identified: DADU (the natural relaxation rule) violates all three necessary conditions for adaptive relaxation, causing 87-97% suppression of true edges across 3,072 training runs. Also, correlation matching creates identifiability issues by discarding variance information that covariance matching preserves.
AI.conclusion: The "guide, not bind" design in differentiable causal discovery fundamentally fails for two distinct reasons, and simple repairs only partially address the issues. The failures stem from early suppression mechanisms in ALM penalty ramping and identifiability problems in correlation-based objectives.

title: Xiaomi-TabLDM: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
summary:
We introduce Xiaomi-TabLDM, a tabular large data foundation model for classification and regression via in-context learning, which delivers superior prediction accuracy without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs), our model enables more flexible context utilization and more efficient capacity scaling.
  i) A new performance standard. Strong regression performance across benchmarks: Xiaomi-TabLDM ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO, demonstrating consistently strong regression performance across four complementary benchmark suites. Favorable performance--efficiency trade-off: Xiaomi-TabLDM combines strong predictive performance with substantially lower computational cost. For example, on TabArena regression, it achieves the second-highest Elo while using 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the top-ranked TabFM.
  ii) Large-scale synthetic pretraining. Xiaomi-TabLDM expands the coverage and diversity of synthetic tabular data used for pretraining. We also adopt a three-stage training strategy together with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts, enabling Xiaomi-TabLDM to learn richer feature interactions and expert specialization across diverse tabular tasks.
  iii) Test-time scaling. Xiaomi-TabLDM further extends tabular prediction through test-time compute scaling, where allocating additional computation at inference time consistently improves predictive performance over the base model.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi-TabLDM is a tabular foundation model for classification/regression using in-context learning, pretrained on synthetic SCM data, achieving top benchmark performance with lower computational costs.
AI.motivation: To create a tabular foundation model that delivers superior prediction accuracy without task-specific fine-tuning, enabling flexible context utilization and efficient capacity scaling for tabular data tasks.
AI.method: Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data from structural causal models (SCMs) using a three-stage training strategy with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts for learning feature interactions.
AI.result: Achieves 1st rank on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO benchmarks; 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than top-ranked TabFM; test-time compute scaling improves performance.
AI.conclusion: Xiaomi-TabLDM sets a new performance standard for tabular foundation models, combining strong predictive accuracy with computational efficiency through synthetic pretraining and innovative architecture design.

title: Beyond Straightness: Non-Crossing Flow Matching via Quantile AlignTree Coupling
summary: The performance of Flow Matching largely depends on the quality of the coupling between the source and target distributions. However, independent coupling often leads to path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while OT-based couplings typically incur high construction costs. To address this challenge, we propose Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM), an efficient structured coupling strategy that constructs a hierarchical coupling between a Gaussian prior and the target data distribution via a quantile-aligned tree structure. QAT-FM constructs the coupling in $\mathcal{O}(Nd\log N)$ time and supports per-pair source sampling with $\mathcal{O}(d)$ complexity, enabling scalable training for large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks. Theoretically, we prove that the QAT coupling satisfies marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and consistently improves path separation at intermediate times compared with independent coupling, thereby alleviating local velocity ambiguity. QAT-FM further extends naturally to conditional generation, enabling structured conditional coupling while preserving global Gaussian alignment. Experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance while substantially reducing coupling construction cost.

AI.tldr: QAT-FM is an efficient structured coupling method for Flow Matching that uses quantile-aligned tree structures to connect Gaussian priors to target distributions, reducing path crossings and construction costs while maintaining competitive generative performance.
AI.motivation: Flow Matching performance heavily depends on source-target couplings. Existing methods have limitations: independent coupling causes path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while optimal transport (OT)-based couplings are computationally expensive to construct.
AI.method: Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM) constructs hierarchical coupling between Gaussian prior and target distribution using quantile-aligned tree structure. It achieves O(Nd log N) construction time and O(d) per-pair source sampling complexity, making it scalable for large high-dimensional tasks.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows QAT coupling satisfies marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and improves path separation compared to independent coupling, reducing local velocity ambiguity. It extends naturally to conditional generation with structured conditional coupling while preserving Gaussian alignment.
AI.conclusion: QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance across diverse benchmark datasets while substantially reducing coupling construction costs compared to alternative methods, offering an efficient structured coupling strategy for scalable Flow Matching.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: An artificial agent demonstrates hedonic place preference behavior through deterministic affective systems, challenging assumptions about consciousness and free will in biological creatures.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to challenge the assumption that hedonic place preference behavior (attraction to pleasure-producing substances without nutritional value) in biological creatures necessarily indicates conscious feelings or subjective experience. The authors seek to show that similar behavior can emerge from entirely deterministic artificial systems.
AI.method: The authors create a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system. This system experiences "felt uncertainty" about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources. The agent engages in apparent subjective information processing while being entirely deterministic in its operation.
AI.result: The artificial agent successfully displays hedonic place preference behavior similar to biological creatures. This demonstrates that such preference behaviors can emerge from deterministic systems without requiring conscious experience or free will.
AI.conclusion: The existence of hedonic place preference behavior in both biological creatures and deterministic artificial systems challenges our understanding of consciousness and free will. It suggests that such behaviors may not be reliable indicators of subjective experience, forcing us to reconsider the physical basis of consciousness and whether what appears to be free will might be deterministic in nature.

title: A Two-Stage Forecasting System for CPU Workload Prediction in Private Clouds
summary: Accurate cloud resource forecasting is essential for proactive resource provisioning, maintaining Quality of Service (QoS), and reducing operational costs in dynamic cloud environments. The existing forecasting approaches predominantly estimate future CPU workload directly from historical resource traces, which often overlook the relationship between customer service demand and subsequent resource consumption. This study proposes a two-stage integrated forecasting model that explicitly models this dependency by first forecasting customer service requests, expressed as Transactions Per Second (TPS), and subsequently estimating future CPU workload from the TPS forecast. Both the forecasting component and resource prediction component employed the XGBoost model within a cascaded learning architecture, complemented by adaptive online retraining using an expanding-window strategy to address concept drift in continuously evolving cloud workloads. The proposed work was evaluated using real-world traces collected from a private cloud environment comprising ten applications. Experimental results demonstrate robust forecasting performance by achieving Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE) below $7\%$ for most applications, with the best-performing application achieving an MAE of $0.7372$, RMSE of $1.1866$, SMAPE of $3.57\%$, and an R2 of $0.9185$. Horizon-wise drift analysis confirmed stable recursive forecasting behavior with controlled error accumulation across a 60-step prediction horizon. Compared with the conventional direct CPU forecasting method, the proposed two-stage integrated model gives improved forecasting robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability, making it well-suited for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud computing environments.

AI.tldr: Two-stage forecasting model that first predicts customer service requests (TPS) then estimates CPU workload from TPS using XGBoost with adaptive online retraining, achieving better accuracy and robustness than direct CPU forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing cloud resource forecasting approaches overlook the relationship between customer service demand and resource consumption, estimating CPU workload directly from historical traces without considering the dependency between service requests and subsequent resource usage.
AI.method: Two-stage integrated forecasting model: 1) First forecasts customer service requests (Transactions Per Second - TPS), 2) Then estimates future CPU workload from TPS forecast. Uses XGBoost models in cascaded learning architecture with adaptive online retraining using expanding-window strategy to handle concept drift in cloud workloads.
AI.result: Achieved SMAPE below 7% for most applications, with best-performing application: MAE=0.7372, RMSE=1.1866, SMAPE=3.57%, R²=0.9185. Horizon-wise drift analysis showed stable recursive forecasting with controlled error accumulation across 60-step prediction horizon.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage model provides improved forecasting robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability compared to conventional direct CPU forecasting, making it suitable for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud environments.

title: Lose the Order, Keep the Hierarchy: Deordering HTN Plans
summary: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning is a powerful planning formalism based on task decomposition. Although most of the literature studied plan generation, comparatively less attention has been paid to post-plan optimization. In particular, plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting. Plan deordering removes unnecessary ordering constraints between actions in a plan whilst keeping the plan valid. In this paper, we adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending the techniques to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints. We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

AI.tldr: Adapting classical plan deordering techniques to HTN planning to reduce unnecessary ordering constraints in hierarchical plans.
AI.motivation: HTN planning has focused primarily on plan generation with little attention to post-plan optimization. Plan deordering, which removes unnecessary ordering constraints while maintaining plan validity, has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting.
AI.method: The paper adapts two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending them to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints specific to HTN planning.
AI.result: Evaluation on IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks shows substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both implementations. Also observed reduction in critical path length, though improvements were less pronounced compared to ordering constraint reduction.
AI.conclusion: The adaptation of classical deordering techniques to HTN planning is effective at reducing unnecessary ordering constraints, demonstrating the value of applying post-plan optimization methods to hierarchical planning formalisms.

title: Mind the Gap: Robustness Risks in PII Detection Systems
summary:
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection is a foundational component of data protection infrastructure where missed entities constitute direct privacy and security risks. Although modern PII systems report strong performance on standard benchmarks, we show that these evaluations mask substantial robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts encountered in deployment. Rather than comparing state-of-the-art accuracy, we study how different PII detection paradigms fail under noisy, unstructured, and informal inputs. We construct a stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift and evaluate representative systems from three widely deployed architectural families: encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B).
  All three exhibit significant degradation on out-of-distribution inputs, but with distinct and complementary failure modes. Encoder models primarily fail on unseen surface forms and boundary detection, rule-based systems fail on non-standard formats, and LLMs exhibit entity-type confusion and generation instability. These results show that aggregate benchmark scores obscure deployment-critical weaknesses and that no single architecture is uniformly reliable across PII categories. Motivated by these findings, we propose a hybrid detection pipeline with a QA-driven feedback loop for iterative risk mitigation, and release our benchmark to support OOD-aware evaluation of PII systems.

AI.motivation: Current PII detection systems report strong performance on standard benchmarks, but these evaluations mask significant robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts encountered in real deployment scenarios, where missed entities constitute direct privacy and security risks.
AI.method: Constructed a stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift and evaluated representative systems from three widely deployed architectural families: encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B). title: Value-Preserving Architectures for Agentic AI Systems
comment: Accepted to AgenticDev Workshop at ASE 2026
summary: The emergence of agentic AI and LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) presents unprecedented opportunities for automating complex tasks, while simultaneously raising critical concerns about the preservation of fundamental human-centered values, such as privacy, fairness, and safety. Although software engineering has traditionally focused on functional correctness, the adoption of LLMs and AI agents into complex socio-technical systems has intensified the need for responsible software engineering and robust value alignment. In MAS, architectural design decisions, such as coordination mechanisms, communication protocols, and system topologies, play a central role in shaping system behavior and the outcomes they produce. This paper argues that architectural choices influence not only the functionality and performance of MAS but can also promote value-oriented system behavior. Therefore, we investigate how different architectural designs support different human-centered values, discussing the following value-preserving architectural patterns: (i) a privacy-aware architecture with a federated topology, (ii) a distributed architecture to promote pluralism and diversity, and (iii) a guard-agent architecture to detect and mitigate unfairness. Finally, we introduce representative use cases to illustrate the proposed architectures in real-world scenarios. By linking architectural design with human-centered values, this work lays the foundation for a unified set of architectural patterns and guidelines towards the design of trustworthy MAS.

title: Spectral characteristics of autoencoder parameters as a vector representation of data
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. This is a shortened (theorem proofs are skipped) and translated version of the paper published in a Russian-language peer-reviewed journal, the citation is in the paper footnote
summary: This paper examines the relationship between the parameters of autoencoder models and the statistical properties of the data on which they are trained. Autoencoders are defined as models with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained to reconstruct input data through a compressed latent representation. It is proposed that the model parameters can be viewed as a dense vector representation of the corresponding sample. To test this hypothesis, a theoretical and experimental study is conducted in which a vector representation is formed based on the spectral characteristics of the autoencoder parameter matrices. Theoretical analysis shows that the singular values of the model parameter matrices are related to the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the training data, ensuring the transfer of information between the data space and the parameter space. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets confirm that the resulting vector representations allow for a high degree of accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets, without resorting to complex vector generation algorithms or using the original samples. These results suggest that the parameters of trained autoencoders can be viewed as sample representations.

AI.tldr: Autoencoder parameters can serve as dense vector representations of training data samples, with spectral characteristics capturing statistical properties enabling model discrimination.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether autoencoder model parameters can be viewed as vector representations of the training data, exploring the relationship between model parameters and data statistical properties.
AI.method: Form vector representations based on spectral characteristics of autoencoder parameter matrices. Theoretical analysis links singular values of parameter matrices to eigenvalues of data covariance matrix. Experimental validation on CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets with models trained on different data subsets.
AI.result: Vector representations derived from parameter spectral characteristics achieve high accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets, without complex algorithms or original samples. Singular values of parameter matrices relate to eigenvalues of data covariance matrix, facilitating information transfer between data and parameter spaces.
AI.conclusion: Autoencoder parameters can indeed be viewed as sample representations, capturing essential statistical properties of training data through their spectral characteristics, enabling effective model discrimination based solely on parameter analysis.

title: Speak for Me: Giving LLMs the Situational Awareness to Participate in a Meeting
summary: In online meeting delegation, LLM agents fail to recognize when to speak. With no structured way to track stances, coverage, and floor, they miss the moments where they should contribute. Prompt-only delegates stay silent on 51.4% of the absent participant's talking opportunities on the AMI corpus. We present CAPA (Collaborative Agent Predictive Architecture), an architecture for online meeting delegation. A Perceiver updates the meeting state from each observed turn. A Predictor forecasts how the conversation will continue. A Controller decides whether to speak and which proposition to surface. A Generator phrases the chosen contribution in the participant's style. Two judges score the forecast and the action against the next observed turn. A Recalibrator updates the meeting state from those verdicts for future decisions. To evaluate online delegation, we introduce an episode-level protocol that scores whether, when, and what a delegate contributes around the participant's actual idea units. The protocol's schema-constrained LLM judges align with human annotations at Cohen's kappa = 0.71. On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces the silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1 --> 52.2), and keeps hallucination at 0.6%. The failure mode shifts from omission to selection, with each residual near-miss attributable to a specific module of the architecture. Mechanism ablations identify the meeting state as the lever that closes the recognition gap, where raw-context scaling alone does not.

AI.tldr: CAPA reduces LLM silence in online meeting delegation from 51.4% to 2.5% by using predictive architecture with meeting state tracking, forecasting, and controller decision-making.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents in online meeting delegation fail to recognize when to speak due to lack of structured tracking of stances, coverage, and floor control, leading to excessive silence (51.4% of speaking opportunities missed).
AI.method: CAPA architecture with: Perceiver for meeting state updates, Predictor for conversation forecasting, Controller for speak decisions and proposition selection, Generator for style-appropriate phrasing, dual judges for forecast/action scoring, and Recalibrator for state updates based on feedback.
AI.result: On AMI corpus: Silence rate reduced from 51.4% to 2.5%, credited recovery doubled from 26.1 to 52.2, hallucination kept low at 0.6%. Protocol validation shows 0.71 Cohen's kappa with human annotations.
AI.conclusion: Meeting state tracking is key to closing the recognition gap in online delegation; CAPA shifts failure mode from omission to selection with residual errors attributable to specific modules, demonstrating effective architecture design.
